decks.title: Carbohydrates — Part 1: Classification and the structure of glucose
goals: Classify carbohydrates by hydrolysis and by reducing power
Explain how six reactions of glucose establish its open-chain structure
Explain why glucose must also exist as a six-membered ring, and what anomers are
Assign D or L configuration to a sugar from its Fischer projection

slides.heading: Sugars, starch and fibre
slides.body_md: Part 1 — what makes a compound a carbohydrate, and how chemists proved the structure of glucose using nothing but test-tube reactions.

visual.alt: Table of everyday materials and the carbohydrate each mainly contains

slides.narration: Namaste! The rice on your plate, the cotton in your shirt and the jaggery in your tea are all carbohydrates. They supply most of our energy and much of the material plants are built from. In this part we classify them and then follow the classic detective story of how the structure of glucose was worked out from its reactions.

slides.heading: Definition and classification
slides.body_md: Carbohydrates are **optically active polyhydroxy aldehydes or ketones**, or substances that give them on hydrolysis. Many fit Cₓ(H₂O)ᵧ, but the formula is not a definition: rhamnose C₆H₁₂O₅ is a carbohydrate, while ethanoic acid C₂H₄O₂ is not. By hydrolysis: **monosaccharides** (no simpler sugar), **oligosaccharides** (2–10 units) and **polysaccharides** (many units). Monosaccharides are **aldoses** (–CHO) or **ketoses** (C=O), named by carbon count: aldopentose, ketohexose.

visual.alt: Table classifying carbohydrates by the number of units obtained on hydrolysis, with examples, taste and solubility

slides.narration: A carbohydrate is an optically active compound with several hydroxyl groups and an aldehyde or ketone group, or one that gives such compounds on hydrolysis. The old idea of a hydrate of carbon is only a rough guide, because some carbohydrates do not fit that formula and some non-carbohydrates do. We sort them by hydrolysis: monosaccharides cannot be split, disaccharides give two units, and polysaccharides give many. Monosaccharides are aldoses or ketoses, named by the number of carbon atoms.

slides.heading: Reducing and non-reducing sugars; importance
slides.body_md: A sugar that reduces **Tollens’ reagent** (silver mirror) or **Fehling’s solution** (red Cu₂O) is a **reducing sugar**: it has a free aldehyde or α-hydroxy ketone group, or a ring that can open to one. All monosaccharides are reducing. A disaccharide is **non-reducing** if both anomeric carbons are tied up in the glycosidic link (sucrose). **Importance:** energy source (glucose, starch, glycogen), structure (cellulose in plants), raw materials (cotton, paper, ethanol by fermentation), and the sugars ribose and deoxyribose in nucleic acids.

visual.alt: Table of six carbohydrates with their response to Tollens’ and Fehling’s reagents and their classification as reducing or non-reducing

slides.narration: Sugars that turn Tollens’ reagent into a silver mirror, or Fehling’s solution into a red precipitate, are reducing sugars. They contain a free aldehyde group, or a ring that can open to give one. Every simple sugar is reducing, but table sugar is not, because its two reactive carbons are locked together. Carbohydrates matter as fuel, as plant structure, as raw materials for cloth, paper and alcohol, and as part of nucleic acids.

slides.heading: Glucose: the open-chain structure
slides.body_md: Glucose, C₆H₁₂O₆, is an **aldohexose**: an unbranched chain of six carbons, –CHO at C1, secondary –OH on C2 to C5 and a primary –CH₂OH at C6. C2, C3, C4 and C5 are chiral, so 2⁴ = 16 stereoisomeric aldohexoses exist; natural glucose is one of them.

slides.narration: Here is glucose drawn as a Fischer projection. Carbon one is an aldehyde group. Carbons two, three, four and five each carry a hydroxyl group and are all chiral, and carbon six is a primary alcohol group. With four chiral carbons there are sixteen possible stereoisomers, and glucose is just one of them. Next we see the reactions that proved this structure.

slides.heading: Evidence 1: the chain and the carbonyl group
slides.body_md: **Molecular formula** C₆H₁₂O₆ from analysis and molar mass. **Prolonged heating with HI** gives **n-hexane**: the six carbons are in a **straight chain**. **Hydroxylamine** gives an oxime and **HCN** a cyanohydrin: a **carbonyl group** is present. **Bromine water** (a mild oxidant) gives **gluconic acid**, C₆H₁₂O₇, with no loss of carbon: the carbonyl is an **aldehyde**.

visual.alt: Table of four reagents, the products they give with glucose and the structural conclusion from each

slides.narration: Heating glucose for a long time with hydrogen iodide strips away all the oxygen and gives normal hexane, so the six carbons form an unbranched chain. Glucose reacts with hydroxylamine to give an oxime and adds hydrogen cyanide, so it has a carbonyl group. Bromine water, a gentle oxidising agent, converts it into gluconic acid with the same six carbons, which can only happen if the carbonyl group is an aldehyde.

slides.heading: Evidence 2: hydroxyl groups and the ends of the chain
slides.body_md: **Acetic anhydride** gives a **pentaacetate**: five –OH groups, on **different carbons** (the compound is stable; one carbon rarely holds two –OH). **Nitric acid** oxidises both ends to **saccharic acid**, HOOC(CHOH)₄COOH, as does nitric acid on gluconic acid: the second end is a **primary alcohol**, –CH₂OH. **Phenylhydrazine** (one mole) gives a phenylhydrazone; with **excess** (three moles) it gives a yellow crystalline **osazone**, involving C1 and C2.

visual.alt: Flow showing bromine water oxidising only the aldehyde end of glucose to give gluconic acid, and nitric acid oxidising both glucose and gluconic acid to saccharic acid

slides.narration: Acetic anhydride converts glucose into a pentaacetate, so there are five hydroxyl groups, each on its own carbon. Nitric acid, a stronger oxidant, turns glucose into saccharic acid, which has an acid group at each end; since gluconic acid gives the same product, the far end must be a primary alcohol group. Phenylhydrazine first gives a phenylhydrazone, and with excess reagent a yellow osazone, in which both carbon one and carbon two have reacted.

slides.heading: Worked example: assembling the structure
slides.body_md:
**Problem.** A hexose X gives n-hexane with HI, an oxime with NH₂OH, a pentaacetate with acetic anhydride and a six-carbon monocarboxylic acid with bromine water. Deduce the open-chain structure of X.

**Step 1.** HI → n-hexane: unbranched chain $\ce{C-C-C-C-C-C}$.

**Step 2.** Oxime: one C=O; bromine water gives an acid with no loss of carbon, so the C=O is –CHO at C1.

**Step 3.** Pentaacetate: five –OH on C2–C6, one each; C6 must be –CH₂OH.

**Result.** $\ce{HOCH2-(CHOH)4-CHO}$, an aldohexose (glucose or one of its stereoisomers).

visual.alt: Flow combining three deductions into the open-chain aldohexose structure

slides.narration: Put the clues together one at a time. Normal hexane from hydrogen iodide fixes an unbranched chain of six carbons. The oxime shows one carbonyl group, and oxidation without losing carbon puts it at the end as an aldehyde. Five acetyl groups mean five hydroxyl groups, one on each remaining carbon, so carbon six is a primary alcohol group. That gives the aldohexose structure, although these reactions cannot tell us the arrangement in space.

slides.heading: Cyclic structure and anomers
slides.body_md: Facts the open chain cannot explain: glucose gives **no Schiff’s test** and **no NaHSO₃ adduct**; the **pentaacetate does not react with NH₂OH**; glucose forms **two crystalline forms** with different rotations; and it forms two isomeric **methyl glucosides**. Explanation: the **C5 –OH adds to the C1 aldehyde**, giving a six-membered **pyranose** ring (a cyclic **hemiacetal**). C1 becomes a new chiral centre (the **anomeric carbon**), so there are two **anomers**, **α** and **β**, differing only at C1. In water each slowly changes to an equilibrium mixture with a trace of open chain: **mutarotation**.

visual.alt: Table comparing alpha and beta D-glucopyranose by position of the anomeric hydroxyl, melting point and specific rotation, and the equilibrium value in water

slides.narration: Some facts do not fit the open chain. Glucose does not restore the colour of Schiff’s reagent, it forms no bisulfite compound, and its pentaacetate has no free aldehyde group. The explanation is that the hydroxyl on carbon five adds to the aldehyde group, closing a six-membered ring called a pyranose. Carbon one becomes a new chiral centre, so two forms exist, alpha and beta, called anomers. In water each slowly turns into the same equilibrium mixture, a change in rotation called mutarotation.

slides.heading: D and L configuration
slides.body_md: D and L describe configuration **relative to glyceraldehyde**. In a Fischer projection with the carbonyl group at the top, look at the **chiral carbon farthest from the C=O** (C5 in a hexose): –OH on the **right** → **D**; on the **left** → **L**. D/L is unrelated to the sign of rotation, which is shown separately as (+) or (−): D-(+)-glucose, but **D-(−)-fructose**.

visual.alt: Table relating the position of the hydroxyl group on the lowest chiral carbon to D or L configuration and showing that the sign of rotation is independent

slides.narration: The letters D and L compare a sugar with glyceraldehyde. Draw the sugar as a Fischer projection with the carbonyl group at the top and look at the chiral carbon farthest from it, which is carbon five in glucose. If its hydroxyl group points right, the sugar belongs to the D series; if left, to the L series. This says nothing about the direction of rotation: natural fructose is D, yet it rotates light to the left.

slides.heading: Worked example: composition of the equilibrium mixture
slides.body_md:
**Problem.** α-D-Glucose has $[\alpha]_D = +111^\circ$ and β-D-glucose $+19.2^\circ$. At equilibrium in water the rotation is $+52.5^\circ$. Ignoring the open chain, find the percentage of the β-anomer.

**Step 1.** Let the fraction of β be $x$: $111(1 - x) + 19.2x = 52.5$.

**Step 2.** $x = \dfrac{111 - 52.5}{111 - 19.2} = \dfrac{58.5}{91.8} = 0.637$.

**Answer.** About **63.7% β** and 36.3% α: the β-anomer, with every –OH equatorial, is more stable.

visual.alt: Table of the rotations of the two anomers, the equilibrium rotation and the calculated fraction of the beta anomer

slides.narration: The equilibrium rotation is a weighted average of the rotations of the two anomers. Call the fraction of beta x, so the fraction of alpha is one minus x. Solving gives x as fifty eight point five divided by ninety one point eight, which is about point six four. So roughly two thirds of dissolved glucose is the beta form, the more stable anomer.

slides.heading: Summary: Part 1
bullets: Carbohydrates: optically active polyhydroxy aldehydes or ketones; mono-, oligo- and polysaccharides; aldoses and ketoses.
Reducing sugars reduce Tollens’ and Fehling’s; sucrose and polysaccharides do not.
Glucose evidence: HI → n-hexane; NH₂OH, HCN → C=O; Br₂ water → gluconic acid (–CHO); pentaacetate (5 –OH); HNO₃ → saccharic acid (–CH₂OH); excess PhNHNH₂ → osazone.
Cyclic pyranose (C5–OH + C1–CHO); α and β anomers at C1; mutarotation to +52.5°.
D/L from the lowest chiral carbon, independent of (+)/(−).

visual.alt: Summary table of four reagents and the feature of glucose each shows

slides.narration: Let us sum up Part 1. Carbohydrates are polyhydroxy aldehydes or ketones, classified by hydrolysis and by whether they reduce Tollens’ and Fehling’s reagents. Six reactions establish the open-chain structure of glucose. A few facts need the six-membered ring, which gives two anomers that interconvert in water. D and L describe configuration at the lowest chiral carbon, not the direction of rotation.

slides.heading: Exam tips: Part 1
bullets: For each reaction, state the reagent, the product and the conclusion — all three earn marks.
Bromine water distinguishes aldehyde from ketone; nitric acid proves the –CH₂OH end.
Anomers differ only at C1; they are diastereomers, not enantiomers.
Never link D with (+) or L with (−).

rows: α and β are mirror images

visual.alt: Table of three common slips in Part 1 and their fixes

slides.narration: Some tips. When asked about the evidence, give the reagent, the product and what it proves. Remember that bromine water picks out the aldehyde group and nitric acid the primary alcohol group. Alpha and beta glucose differ at carbon one only, so they are not mirror images. And keep the letters D and L separate from the plus and minus signs of rotation.

decks.title: Carbohydrates — Part 2: Fructose, disaccharides and polysaccharides
goals: Describe the open-chain and cyclic structures of fructose
Use the bromine-water test to distinguish glucose from fructose
Identify the units and glycosidic links in sucrose, maltose and lactose
Compare starch, cellulose and glycogen in structure and function

slides.heading: From fruit sugar to fibre
slides.body_md: Part 2 — the ketose fructose, the three common disaccharides and the giant glucose polymers.

visual.alt: Flow showing monosaccharides joining by glycosidic links with loss of water to form disaccharides and then polysaccharides

slides.narration: In Part 2 we meet fructose, the sugar of fruit and honey, and learn a simple test to tell it from glucose. Then we see how sugar units join through glycosidic links, losing water each time, to give the disaccharides sucrose, maltose and lactose, and finally the polysaccharides starch, cellulose and glycogen.

slides.heading: Fructose: open chain and ring
slides.body_md: **Fructose**, C₆H₁₂O₆, is a **ketohexose**: HOCH₂–CO–(CHOH)₃–CH₂OH, with the ketone at **C2**. Like glucose it gives n-hexane with HI and a pentaacetate. Its cyanohydrin, hydrolysed and reduced with HI, gives **2-methylhexanoic acid**, which places the C=O at C2 (glucose gives straight-chain heptanoic acid). In solution the **C5 –OH adds to C2**, giving a five-membered **furanose** ring (a hemiketal) with α and β anomers. Natural fructose is **D-(−)**, laevorotatory, [α]D = −92.4°.

visual.alt: Flow converting fructose through its cyanohydrin and hydroxy acid into 2-methylhexanoic acid, showing a branch at carbon 2

slides.narration: Fructose has the same formula as glucose, but its carbonyl group is a ketone at carbon two. Adding hydrogen cyanide, hydrolysing and then reducing with hydrogen iodide gives two-methylhexanoic acid, with a branch at carbon two, while glucose gives an unbranched acid. In solution fructose closes a five-membered ring, called a furanose, by joining the hydroxyl on carbon five to carbon two. It is laevorotatory.

slides.heading: The bromine-water test
slides.body_md: **Bromine water** is a mild oxidant that attacks **aldehydes** but not ketones (and it is not alkaline, so fructose cannot rearrange). **Glucose** decolourises the orange-brown bromine water, forming gluconic acid; **fructose** does not. Tollens’ and Fehling’s **cannot** distinguish them: in alkaline solution fructose isomerises (via an enediol) and so is also a reducing sugar. Both give the **same osazone**, because only C1 and C2 react and the two sugars have the same configuration at C3–C5.

visual.alt: Table comparing glucose and fructose in four tests

slides.narration: Bromine water is the way to tell glucose from fructose. It oxidises an aldehyde group but not a ketone, and because it is not alkaline, fructose cannot first rearrange into an aldose. So glucose decolourises bromine water and fructose leaves it orange. Fehling’s solution and Tollens’ reagent do not help, because both sugars reduce them, and both give the same osazone.

slides.heading: Worked example: two unlabelled sugar solutions
slides.body_md:
**Problem.** Bottles P and Q contain glucose and fructose solutions. Both give a red precipitate with Fehling’s solution. P decolourises bromine water; Q does not. Identify P and Q and write the equation for the positive test.

**Step 1.** Both are reducing sugars, so Fehling’s cannot separate them.

**Step 2.** Only an aldose is oxidised by bromine water: **P is glucose**, **Q is fructose**.

**Step 3.** $\ce{HOCH2(CHOH)4CHO + Br2 + H2O -> HOCH2(CHOH)4COOH + 2HBr}$

visual.alt: Table of results for bottles P and Q and the sugar identified

slides.narration: Both bottles give a red precipitate with Fehling’s solution, so that test alone cannot separate them. Bromine water oxidises only the aldehyde group, so the bottle that decolourises it, P, contains glucose, and Q contains fructose. The product from P is gluconic acid.

slides.heading: Quick check: glucose or fructose?
slides.body_md: Choose the test or observation that distinguishes glucose from fructose.
slides.narration: Quick check. Remember which reagent attacks only aldehyde groups and is not alkaline.

slides.heading: Sucrose
slides.body_md: Two monosaccharides join through a **glycosidic linkage**, C–O–C, formed from a hemiacetal –OH and an –OH of another sugar with loss of water. **Sucrose**, C₁₂H₂₂O₁₁: **α-D-glucopyranose (C1)** linked to **β-D-fructofuranose (C2)** — an **α1→β2** link joining the two anomeric carbons. No hemiacetal remains, so sucrose is **non-reducing** and shows no mutarotation. Hydrolysis (dilute acid or **invertase**) changes the rotation from +66.5° to about −20°: the product is **invert sugar**.

visual.alt: Table of the units, link, ring sizes, reducing behaviour and rotation of sucrose

slides.narration: Sugar units join through a glycosidic linkage, an oxygen bridge formed with loss of water. In sucrose, carbon one of alpha glucose is joined to carbon two of beta fructose, so both reducing carbons are used up. That is why cane sugar is non-reducing and shows no mutarotation. When it is hydrolysed, the rotation changes from positive to negative, so the product is called invert sugar.

slides.heading: Maltose and lactose
slides.body_md: **Maltose** (malt sugar, from starch by the enzyme diastase): two **α-D-glucose** units, **C1 of one to C4 of the next** (α-1,4 link). **Lactose** (milk sugar): **β-D-galactose C1** linked to **C4 of D-glucose** (β-1,4 link). In both, the second unit keeps a free hemiacetal –OH at its C1, so both are **reducing** and show mutarotation.

visual.alt: Table comparing sucrose, maltose and lactose by units, glycosidic link, reducing power and hydrolysing enzyme

slides.narration: Maltose is formed when the enzyme diastase breaks down starch. It contains two alpha glucose units joined from carbon one of the first to carbon four of the second. Lactose, the sugar of milk, contains beta galactose joined from its carbon one to carbon four of glucose. In both, the second unit keeps a free hemiacetal group, so maltose and lactose are reducing sugars.

slides.heading: Worked example: identifying a disaccharide
slides.body_md:
**Problem.** A disaccharide Y reduces Tollens’ reagent. Enzymic hydrolysis gives only D-glucose, and the enzyme used acts only on α-glycosidic links. Identify Y and describe its link.

**Step 1.** Only glucose on hydrolysis: Y is maltose or a glucose–glucose disaccharide (not sucrose or lactose).

**Step 2.** Reducing: one anomeric carbon is free, so the link is C1 → C4, not C1 → C1.

**Step 3.** α-specific enzyme: the link is α.

**Answer.** Y is **maltose**, an α-1,4 glycosidic link between two D-glucose units.

visual.alt: Flow combining three observations to identify maltose

slides.narration: Use each clue in turn. Getting only glucose rules out sucrose and lactose. Reducing Tollens’ reagent means one anomeric carbon is still free, so the link runs from carbon one to carbon four. An enzyme that cuts only alpha links shows the link is alpha. Together these identify maltose.

slides.heading: Starch
slides.body_md: **Starch**, (C₆H₁₀O₅)ₙ, is the energy store of plants: a mixture of **amylose** (15–20%; long **unbranched** chains of α-D-glucose with **α-1,4** links; soluble in hot water; deep **blue with iodine**) and **amylopectin** (80–85%; α-1,4 chains **branched by α-1,6 links** about every 20–25 units; insoluble; red-violet with iodine). Acid hydrolysis gives dextrins, then maltose, then glucose.

visual.alt: Flow of the stepwise hydrolysis of starch through dextrins and maltose to glucose

slides.narration: Starch is how plants store glucose. About a fifth is amylose, long unbranched chains of alpha glucose that give the deep blue colour with iodine. The rest is amylopectin, whose chains branch through carbon six roughly every twenty to twenty five units. Hydrolysis breaks starch down step by step into dextrins, then maltose, and finally glucose.

slides.heading: Cellulose and glycogen
slides.body_md: **Cellulose**: unbranched chains of **β-D-glucose** joined by **β-1,4** links; neighbouring chains are held by many **hydrogen bonds** into strong fibres — the main material of plant cell walls (cotton is nearly pure cellulose). Humans lack the enzyme for β-links, so cellulose is dietary fibre; cattle digest it with the help of gut microbes. **Glycogen** (animal starch): α-D-glucose with α-1,4 chains and **α-1,6 branches about every 8–12 units**, more branched than amylopectin; stored in **liver and muscle** and quickly broken down to glucose.

visual.alt: Table comparing starch, cellulose and glycogen by unit, links, branching, role and digestibility

slides.narration: Cellulose is also made of glucose, but beta glucose. Its straight chains lie side by side and hydrogen bond to one another, making tough fibres such as cotton. We have no enzyme for beta links, so cellulose passes through us as fibre, although cattle use gut microbes to digest it. Glycogen is the animal store, like amylopectin but even more branched, kept in the liver and muscles.

slides.heading: Worked example: glucose from starch
slides.body_md:
**Problem.** A mill hydrolyses $32.4\ \text{kg}$ of pure starch completely. What mass of glucose ($M = 180$) can be formed? (One chain unit, $\ce{C6H10O5}$, has $M = 162$.)

**Step 1.** Moles of units $= \dfrac{32400}{162} = 200\ \text{mol}$.

**Step 2.** Each unit gives one glucose: mass $= 200 \times 180 = 36000\ \text{g} = 36.0\ \text{kg}$.

The mass rises because each unit takes up one $\ce{H2O}$.

visual.alt: Table of the starch mass, moles of chain units and mass of glucose formed

notes.title: Carbohydrates — Notes

sections.heading: 1. Definition and classification
sections.body_md:
**Carbohydrates:** optically active polyhydroxy aldehydes or ketones, or compounds giving them on hydrolysis. The formula Cₓ(H₂O)ᵧ is only a rough guide (rhamnose C₆H₁₂O₅ is a carbohydrate; ethanoic acid C₂H₄O₂ is not).

**By hydrolysis:** monosaccharides (glucose, fructose, ribose) → oligosaccharides (2–10 units: sucrose, maltose, lactose) → polysaccharides (starch, cellulose, glycogen). **Aldoses** (–CHO) and **ketoses** (C=O), named by carbon count (aldohexose, ketohexose, aldopentose). Mono- and disaccharides are sweet, soluble **sugars**; polysaccharides are **non-sugars**.

**Reducing sugars** reduce Tollens’ and Fehling’s (free aldehyde or α-hydroxy ketone, or a ring that opens to one): all monosaccharides, maltose, lactose. **Non-reducing:** sucrose, polysaccharides.

**Importance:** energy (glucose, starch, glycogen), structure (cellulose), materials (cotton, paper, ethanol), ribose and deoxyribose in nucleic acids.

key_terms.definition_md: A carbohydrate that cannot be hydrolysed to a simpler sugar.
A sugar that reduces Tollens’ reagent and Fehling’s solution because it has a free (or potentially free) carbonyl group.

visual.alt: Table of four carbohydrates with class and reducing behaviour

sections.heading: 2. Structure of glucose
sections.body_md:
**Open chain** HOCH₂(CHOH)₄CHO (aldohexose; C2–C5 chiral; 2⁴ = 16 stereoisomers). Evidence:

| Reagent | Product | Shows |
|---|---|---|
| HI, prolonged heating | n-Hexane | Straight C₆ chain |
| NH₂OH / HCN | Oxime / cyanohydrin | C=O group |
| Br₂ water | Gluconic acid (C₆) | C=O is –CHO |
| (CH₃CO)₂O | Pentaacetate | Five –OH, on different carbons |
| HNO₃ | Saccharic acid HOOC(CHOH)₄COOH | Primary –CH₂OH |
| C₆H₅NHNH₂ (1 mol / 3 mol) | Phenylhydrazone / osazone | C=O; C1 and C2 react |

**Cyclic (pyranose) structure:** C5–OH adds to C1–CHO (hemiacetal). Explains: no Schiff’s test, no NaHSO₃ adduct, pentaacetate unreactive to NH₂OH, two crystalline forms, two methyl glucosides. C1 is the **anomeric carbon**: **α** (+111°, m.p. 419 K) and **β** (+19.2°, 423 K); **mutarotation** to +52.5° (about 36% α, 64% β).

**D/L:** –OH on the lowest chiral carbon (C5) right = D, left = L (relative to glyceraldehyde); independent of (+)/(−).

key_terms.definition_md: Cyclic stereoisomers of a sugar that differ only in configuration at the anomeric carbon (C1 of glucose).
The gradual change in specific rotation of a freshly prepared solution of one anomer to a constant equilibrium value.

visual.alt: Table of rotations of the glucose anomers

sections.heading: 3. Fructose and the bromine-water test
sections.body_md:
**Fructose:** ketohexose HOCH₂CO(CHOH)₃CH₂OH, C=O at **C2**; gives n-hexane with HI; cyanohydrin → hydrolysis → HI gives **2-methylhexanoic acid** (glucose gives heptanoic acid). Ring: C5–OH + C2 → five-membered **furanose** (α and β anomers). **D-(−)**, −92.4°.

Fructose reduces Tollens’ and Fehling’s (it isomerises in alkali), and gives the **same osazone** as glucose. **Bromine water** (mild, not alkaline) oxidises **glucose** (decolourised) but **not fructose**:

$\ce{HOCH2(CHOH)4CHO + Br2 + H2O -> HOCH2(CHOH)4COOH + 2HBr}$

key_terms.definition_md: A five-membered ring form of a sugar containing four carbons and one oxygen.
A monosaccharide containing a ketone group.

visual.alt: Table of bromine-water and Fehling’s results for glucose and fructose

sections.heading: 4. Disaccharides
sections.body_md:
**Glycosidic linkage:** C–O–C link formed between the anomeric –OH of one sugar and an –OH of another, with loss of water.

| Disaccharide | Units | Link | Reducing? |
|---|---|---|---|
| Sucrose | α-D-glucose + β-D-fructose | C1 (Glc) – C2 (Fru), α1→β2 | No |
| Maltose | 2 α-D-glucose | α-1,4 | Yes |
| Lactose | β-D-galactose + D-glucose | β-1,4 | Yes |

Sucrose (+66.5°) hydrolyses (H⁺ or invertase) to an equimolar glucose + fructose mixture of rotation about −20°: **invert sugar**. Maltose comes from starch (diastase) and lactose from milk.

key_terms.definition_md: The ether (C–O–C) link joining two monosaccharide units through an anomeric carbon.
The equimolar mixture of glucose and fructose formed by hydrolysis of sucrose; laevorotatory although sucrose is dextrorotatory.

visual.alt: Table of disaccharide links

sections.heading: 5. Polysaccharides
sections.body_md:
**Starch** (plants): **amylose** 15–20% (unbranched α-1,4, water-soluble, blue with I₂) + **amylopectin** 80–85% (α-1,4 chains branched by α-1,6 about every 20–25 units, insoluble). Hydrolysis: starch → dextrins → maltose → glucose.

**Cellulose** (cell walls, cotton): unbranched **β-1,4** chains, hydrogen-bonded into fibres; not digested by humans (no enzyme for β-links); digested by ruminants with gut microbes.

**Glycogen** (liver, muscle): α-1,4 with α-1,6 branches about every 8–12 units — more branched than amylopectin.

Mass relation: each chain unit C₆H₁₀O₅ (162) gives one glucose (180).

key_terms.definition_md: The branched, water-insoluble component of starch with α-1,4 and α-1,6 links.
The highly branched glucose polymer that stores energy in animals.

visual.alt: Table comparing three polysaccharides

notes.exam_tips_md:
**Common mistakes**
- Using Fehling’s solution to distinguish glucose from fructose (both are positive; use bromine water).
- Calling α- and β-glucose enantiomers (they are anomers, differing at C1 only).
- Linking D with (+).
- Writing lactose as glucose + glucose, or giving cellulose α-links.

**How marks are usually awarded**
- Evidence for glucose structure (1 mark per reaction): reagent, product and conclusion.
- Disaccharide structure (2 marks): units, carbons joined, α/β, reducing or not.
- Polysaccharide comparisons (3 marks): one point each for unit, link/branching and function.

questions.stem_md: Raffinose, a sugar in beans, gives one molecule each of galactose, glucose and fructose on complete hydrolysis and does not reduce Fehling’s solution. Raffinose is best described as:
questions.solution_md: Three units → oligosaccharide; no reaction with Fehling’s → non-reducing — option (b).

questions.stem_md: Which compound can be written as Cₓ(H₂O)ᵧ but is NOT a carbohydrate?
questions.solution_md: Lactic acid fits C₃(H₂O)₃ but is a hydroxy acid, not a polyhydroxy aldehyde or ketone — option (d).

questions.stem_md: Dihydroxyacetone, HOCH₂COCH₂OH, the active ingredient of sunless tanning lotions, is the simplest:
questions.solution_md: Three carbons and a ketone group — option (d).

questions.stem_md: True or false? Every monosaccharide, whether an aldose or a ketose, reduces Fehling’s solution.
questions.solution_md: True: aldoses have –CHO; ketoses such as fructose isomerise in alkali and also reduce it.

questions.stem_md: A carbohydrate that yields between two and ten monosaccharide units on hydrolysis is called an ___.
questions.solution_md: **Oligosaccharide**.

questions.stem_md: Match each carbohydrate with its correct description.
questions.solution_md: Galactose → aldohexose; lactose → reducing disaccharide; sucrose → non-reducing disaccharide; glycogen → branched polysaccharide.

questions.stem_md: Classify each of the following as a mono-, di- or polysaccharide, and as reducing or non-reducing: (a) maltose, (b) cellulose, (c) fructose, (d) sucrose.

answer.model_answer_md: (a) Maltose: disaccharide, reducing. (b) Cellulose: polysaccharide, non-reducing. (c) Fructose: monosaccharide, reducing. (d) Sucrose: disaccharide, non-reducing.

questions.solution_md: Four classifications.

questions.stem_md: (a) Define carbohydrates, and use rhamnose (C₆H₁₂O₅) and ethanoic acid (C₂H₄O₂) to show why “hydrates of carbon” is not a satisfactory definition. (b) Distinguish between sugars and non-sugars, with one example of each. (c) State two uses of carbohydrates other than as food.

answer.model_answer_md: (a) Optically active polyhydroxy aldehydes or ketones, or compounds that give them on hydrolysis. Rhamnose is a carbohydrate but does not fit Cₓ(H₂O)ᵧ; ethanoic acid fits C₂(H₂O)₂ but is not a carbohydrate. (b) Sugars (mono- and disaccharides) are crystalline, sweet and water-soluble, e.g. sucrose; non-sugars (polysaccharides) are amorphous, tasteless and mostly insoluble, e.g. starch. (c) Cellulose for cotton textiles and paper; fermentation of starch or molasses to ethanol (also: wood for furniture, glucose drips).

questions.solution_md: Definition with counter-examples; sugars vs non-sugars; two uses.

questions.stem_md: Four unlabelled solutions contain glucose, fructose, sucrose and starch. Using only iodine solution, Fehling’s solution and bromine water, describe how you would identify each, giving the observations.

answer.model_answer_md: Iodine: only starch gives a blue-black colour. Fehling’s on the other three: sucrose gives no red precipitate (non-reducing); glucose and fructose both give red Cu₂O. Bromine water on these two: glucose decolourises it (oxidised to gluconic acid); fructose leaves it orange-brown.

questions.solution_md: Iodine → starch; Fehling’s → sucrose; bromine water → glucose vs fructose.

marking_scheme.step: Glucose vs fructose by bromine water

questions.stem_md: Glucose gives n-hexane when heated for a long time with hydrogen iodide. This shows that glucose:

options.text_md: has its six carbon atoms in an unbranched chain

questions.solution_md: n-Hexane is the straight-chain C₆ alkane — option (b).

questions.stem_md: D-Glucose is warmed with three moles of phenylhydrazine and gives a yellow osazone. The carbon atoms of glucose that take part are:
questions.solution_md: C1 (aldehyde) and the adjacent C2 (oxidised to C=O by the second mole) each form =N–NHC₆H₅ — option (a).

questions.stem_md: How many moles of acetic anhydride are needed to convert one mole of D-glucose completely into its acetyl ester?
questions.solution_md: Five –OH groups, one acetic anhydride each — option (b).

questions.stem_md: D-Glucose is oxidised to acid X by nitric acid and to acid Y by bromine water. Which statement about X and Y is correct?

options.text_md: X and Y are both gluconic acid
X has five carbons because nitric acid removes C1
X is a dicarboxylic acid (saccharic acid) and Y a monocarboxylic acid (gluconic acid), both with six carbons
Y is a dicarboxylic acid and X a monocarboxylic acid

questions.solution_md: Bromine water oxidises only –CHO; nitric acid also oxidises –CH₂OH — option (c).

questions.stem_md: In the Fischer projection of a hexose, drawn with the carbonyl group at the top, the –OH on the chiral carbon farthest from the carbonyl group points to the left. The sugar:

options.text_md: belongs to the L series, whatever its sign of rotation

questions.solution_md: D/L is fixed by configuration relative to glyceraldehyde, not by rotation — option (a).

questions.stem_md: When the C5 hydroxyl group of D-glucose adds to the C1 aldehyde group to close the pyranose ring, which carbon atom becomes a new chiral centre?
questions.solution_md: C1 gains an –OH and an –O– ring bond, becoming the anomeric carbon — option (a).

questions.stem_md: D-Glucose does not form an addition compound with sodium hydrogensulfite, although its open-chain formula has an aldehyde group. The best explanation is that:

options.text_md: in solution almost all glucose exists as the cyclic hemiacetal, with only a trace of free aldehyde
the aldehyde group of glucose is hindered by five –OH groups
sodium hydrogensulfite oxidises glucose to gluconic acid

questions.solution_md: The aldehyde is tied up in the ring — option (a).

questions.stem_md: A freshly prepared solution of pure β-D-glucose is placed in a polarimeter and observed for several hours. Its specific rotation:

options.text_md: changes slowly to a negative value
rises slowly from +19.2° to a steady +52.5°

questions.solution_md: β converts partly to α until equilibrium (mutarotation) — option (d).

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** Prolonged heating of glucose with HI gives n-hexane.

**Reason (R):** Glucose has an aldehyde group at C1.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: Both are true, but the formation of n-hexane shows the straight chain, not the aldehyde group — option (b).

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** D-Glucose can be obtained in two crystalline forms with different melting points and specific rotations.

**Reason (R):** Ring closure makes C1 of glucose a new chiral centre, giving two anomers.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: Both are true, and R explains A — option (a).

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** D-Fructose is laevorotatory.

**Reason (R):** The letter D shows that a sugar rotates plane-polarised light to the right.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: A is true; R is false: D refers to configuration, not rotation — option (c).

questions.stem_md: True or false? During mutarotation, α-D-glucose is converted into its enantiomer.
questions.solution_md: False: α and β are anomers (diastereomers differing at C1), not enantiomers.

questions.stem_md: The six-membered ring form of glucose, containing five carbon atoms and one oxygen atom, is called the ___ form.
questions.solution_md: **Pyranose**.

questions.stem_md: Match each reagent used in proving the structure of D-glucose with the product it forms.
questions.solution_md: HI → n-hexane; NH₂OH → oxime; acetic anhydride → pentaacetate; HNO₃ → saccharic acid.

questions.stem_md: How many stereoisomers are possible for an open-chain aldohexose, HOCH₂(CHOH)₄CHO, which has four different chiral carbon atoms?

α-D-Glucose has $[\alpha]_D = +111^\circ$ and β-D-glucose $+19.2^\circ$; an equilibrium solution in water shows $+52.5^\circ$. Ignoring the open-chain form, what percentage of the dissolved glucose is the β-anomer?
$3.60\ \text{g}$ of glucose ($M = 180$) is converted completely into glucose pentaacetate, $\ce{C16H22O11}$ ($M = 390$). What mass of the pentaacetate is formed?

What is the minimum mass of phenylhydrazine ($M = 108$) needed to convert $9.00\ \text{g}$ of glucose ($M = 180$) completely into its osazone? ($\ce{C6H12O6 + 3C6H5NHNH2 -> C18H22N4O4 + C6H5NH2 + NH3 + 2H2O}$)
questions.solution_md: $n(\text{glucose}) = 9.00 \div 180 = 0.0500\ \text{mol}$; phenylhydrazine $= 3 \times 0.0500 = 0.150\ \text{mol}$; mass $= 0.150 \times 108 = 16.2\ \text{g}$.

questions.stem_md: Write equations for the reactions of D-glucose with (a) hydroxylamine and (b) bromine water, and state what each reaction shows about its structure.

answer.model_answer_md: (a) $\ce{HOCH2(CHOH)4CHO + NH2OH -> HOCH2(CHOH)4CH=NOH + H2O}$: a carbonyl group is present. (b) $\ce{HOCH2(CHOH)4CHO + Br2 + H2O -> HOCH2(CHOH)4COOH + 2HBr}$: gluconic acid has the same six carbons, so the carbonyl is an aldehyde.

questions.solution_md: Oxime → C=O; gluconic acid → –CHO.

questions.stem_md: Explain what “D” and “(+)” mean in the name D-(+)-glucose. Why is natural fructose written as D-(−)-fructose?

answer.model_answer_md: D: in the Fischer projection, the –OH on the chiral carbon farthest from the carbonyl (C5) is on the right, as in D-glyceraldehyde — a statement about configuration. (+): the sugar rotates plane-polarised light to the right (dextrorotatory). Fructose has the same configuration at C5 (D) but is laevorotatory, so it is D-(−); the two labels are independent.

questions.solution_md: D = configuration; (+) = rotation; independent.

questions.stem_md: What are anomers? Using rotation values, describe what happens when crystals of α-D-glucose are dissolved in water and the solution is left to stand.

answer.model_answer_md: Anomers are cyclic stereoisomers that differ only in configuration at the anomeric carbon (C1 of glucose). A fresh solution of α-D-glucose shows +111°; the ring opens and closes, forming β until equilibrium, and the rotation falls to a constant +52.5° (mutarotation).

questions.solution_md: Definition; +111° → +52.5°.

questions.stem_md: (a) Name the two groups in open-chain D-glucose that react to form the pyranose ring, and the type of compound formed. (b) Explain why methyl α-D-glucoside, formed with methanol and dry HCl, does not reduce Fehling’s solution, although glucose does. (c) Explain why a solution of glucose shows mutarotation but a solution of methyl α-D-glucoside does not.

answer.model_answer_md: (a) The C5 –OH adds to the C1 –CHO, forming a cyclic hemiacetal. (b) In the glucoside the anomeric –OH is replaced by –OCH₃ (an acetal), so the ring cannot open to give a free aldehyde; glucose itself has a hemiacetal that opens in alkaline Fehling’s. (c) Mutarotation needs the ring to open and re-close at C1, which a hemiacetal can do; the glucoside is an acetal, locked as one anomer, so its rotation stays constant.

questions.solution_md: Hemiacetal; acetal cannot open; no ring opening, no mutarotation.

questions.stem_md: D-Glucose is treated separately with (a) acetic anhydride, (b) concentrated nitric acid and (c) excess phenylhydrazine. For each, name the product and state what it reveals about glucose.

answer.model_answer_md: (a) Glucose pentaacetate: five –OH groups, each on a different carbon. (b) Saccharic acid, HOOC(CHOH)₄COOH: besides –CHO there is a primary –CH₂OH group at the other end of the chain. (c) Glucosazone: the carbonyl group is at C1 next to a –CHOH group (C1 and C2 react).

questions.solution_md: Pentaacetate; saccharic acid; osazone.

questions.stem_md: α-D-Galactose has a specific rotation of $+150.7^\circ$ and β-D-galactose $+52.8^\circ$; an equilibrium solution in water shows $+80.2^\circ$. (a) Name the phenomenon. (b) Calculate the percentage of the β-anomer at equilibrium, ignoring the open chain. (c) Which anomer is more stable in water?

answer.model_answer_md: (a) Mutarotation. (b) $150.7(1 - x) + 52.8x = 80.2$, so $x = \dfrac{150.7 - 80.2}{150.7 - 52.8} = \dfrac{70.5}{97.9} = 0.720$: about 72.0% β. (c) The β-anomer, which predominates.

questions.solution_md: Mutarotation; 72.0% β; β more stable.

questions.stem_md:
(a) Describe the reactions of D-glucose with (i) HI, (ii) hydroxylamine and (iii) bromine water, and state what each shows about its open-chain structure. [3]

(b) Give two observations that the open-chain structure cannot explain. [1]

(c) What does the letter D in D-glucose signify? [1]

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) (i) Prolonged heating with HI gives n-hexane: six carbons in an unbranched chain. (ii) $\ce{HOCH2(CHOH)4CHO + NH2OH -> HOCH2(CHOH)4CH=NOH + H2O}$: a carbonyl group. (iii) $\ce{HOCH2(CHOH)4CHO + Br2 + H2O -> HOCH2(CHOH)4COOH + 2HBr}$: no carbon lost, so the carbonyl is an aldehyde.

(b) Any two: no Schiff’s test; no NaHSO₃ adduct; the pentaacetate does not react with NH₂OH; two crystalline forms (α and β) with different rotations; mutarotation.

(c) In the Fischer projection, the –OH on C5 (lowest chiral carbon) is on the right, as in D-glyceraldehyde.

questions.solution_md: Three reactions with inferences; two anomalies; meaning of D.

questions.stem_md: A laboratory assistant has two unlabelled bottles, one of glucose solution and one of fructose solution. Which reagent will tell them apart?
questions.solution_md: Only glucose decolourises bromine water; both reduce Fehling’s and Tollens’ and give the same osazone — option (c).

questions.stem_md: The five-membered ring of D-fructose, as found in sucrose, is formed by reaction between:

options.text_md: the C5 –OH and a C1 aldehyde group
the C5 –OH and the C2 ketone group
the C6 –OH and the C2 ketone group
the C4 –OH and the C1 –CH₂OH group

questions.solution_md: A hemiketal from C5–OH and C2=O gives a ring of four carbons and one oxygen — option (b).

questions.stem_md: Fructose is converted to its cyanohydrin, which is hydrolysed and then heated with HI. The final product is:
questions.solution_md: The new –COOH is on C2, so it forms a branch: CH₃(CH₂)₃CH(CH₃)COOH — option (b).

questions.stem_md: Fructose, a ketose, still reduces Fehling’s solution because:

options.text_md: its ketone group is oxidised directly to a carboxylic acid
its furanose ring contains an aldehyde group
in the alkaline reagent it isomerises through an enediol to aldoses, which are oxidised
it is hydrolysed by Fehling’s solution to glucose

questions.solution_md: Alkali causes keto–enol rearrangement (Lobry de Bruyn–van Ekenstein) — option (c).

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** Tollens’ reagent can be used to distinguish glucose from fructose.

**Reason (R):** Fructose is a reducing sugar.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: A is false (both give a silver mirror); R is true — option (d).

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** Bromine water oxidises glucose but not fructose.

**Reason (R):** Bromine water is a mild oxidant that is not alkaline, so it attacks an aldehyde group but cannot first convert a ketose into an aldose.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: Both are true, and R explains A — option (a).

questions.stem_md: True or false? D-Glucose and D-fructose give the same osazone with excess phenylhydrazine.
questions.solution_md: True: only C1 and C2 react, and C3–C5 are identical in the two sugars.

questions.stem_md: Because it turns plane-polarised light to the left, natural fructose is described as ___ (dextrorotatory or laevorotatory).
questions.solution_md: **Laevorotatory**.

questions.stem_md: A solution containing $0.900\ \text{g}$ of glucose ($M = 180$) is oxidised completely by bromine water. What mass of bromine, $\ce{Br2}$ ($M = 160$), is used? ($\ce{HOCH2(CHOH)4CHO + Br2 + H2O -> HOCH2(CHOH)4COOH + 2HBr}$)
Write the open-chain formula of fructose, and explain how the formation of 2-methylhexanoic acid (via the cyanohydrin, hydrolysis and HI) proves the position of its carbonyl group.

answer.model_answer_md: HOCH₂–CO–(CHOH)₃–CH₂OH. HCN adds at the C=O; the –CN becomes –COOH and HI removes all –OH groups. A branch (–COOH) appears on C2 of a six-carbon chain, so the C=O was at C2 (glucose, with C=O at C1, gives unbranched heptanoic acid).

questions.solution_md: Formula; branch on C2.

questions.stem_md: Give a chemical test, with an equation, to distinguish glucose from fructose, and explain why Fehling’s solution cannot be used for this purpose.

answer.model_answer_md: Bromine water: glucose decolourises it, fructose does not. $\ce{HOCH2(CHOH)4CHO + Br2 + H2O -> HOCH2(CHOH)4COOH + 2HBr}$. Fehling’s is alkaline; fructose isomerises in alkali to aldoses and so reduces it too — both give red Cu₂O.

questions.solution_md: Bromine water; both reduce Fehling’s.

questions.stem_md: Compare glucose and fructose with respect to (a) the type and position of the carbonyl group, (b) the size of the ring in the cyclic form and (c) their behaviour with bromine water.

answer.model_answer_md: (a) Glucose: aldehyde at C1 (aldohexose); fructose: ketone at C2 (ketohexose). (b) Glucose: six-membered pyranose (C5–OH + C1); fructose: five-membered furanose (C5–OH + C2). (c) Glucose decolourises bromine water (→ gluconic acid); fructose does not react.

questions.solution_md: Carbonyl; ring; bromine water.

questions.stem_md:
(a) Write the open-chain structure of D-fructose and describe how its cyclic structure is formed, naming the ring type. [2]

(b) Describe, with an equation, a test to distinguish glucose from fructose. [2]

(c) Why do glucose and fructose give the same osazone? [1]

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) HOCH₂–CO–(CHOH)₃–CH₂OH (ketohexose, C=O at C2). The C5 –OH adds to the C2 ketone, giving a five-membered furanose ring (cyclic hemiketal) with α and β anomers.

(b) Bromine water: decolourised by glucose only. $\ce{HOCH2(CHOH)4CHO + Br2 + H2O -> HOCH2(CHOH)4COOH + 2HBr}$.

(c) Only C1 and C2 react with phenylhydrazine; the configurations at C3, C4 and C5 are the same in both sugars.

questions.solution_md: Structure and furanose; bromine water; C1–C2 only.

questions.stem_md: Maltose, formed when the enzyme diastase acts on starch, contains two glucose units joined by:
questions.solution_md: C1 of one α-D-glucose to C4 of the next — option (b).

questions.stem_md: Sucrose does not reduce Tollens’ reagent because its glycosidic link joins:

options.text_md: C1 of α-D-glucose to C2 of β-D-fructose, using both anomeric carbons
C1 of α-D-glucose to C4 of D-fructose
C1 of β-D-galactose to C4 of D-glucose
C1 of α-D-glucose to C6 of D-fructose

questions.solution_md: No free hemiacetal or hemiketal remains — option (a).

questions.stem_md: Lactose, the sugar of milk, contains a glycosidic link between:

options.text_md: C1 of α-D-glucose and C2 of β-D-fructose
C1 of α-D-glucose and C4 of D-glucose
C1 of β-D-galactose and C4 of D-glucose
C1 of β-D-glucose and C6 of D-galactose

questions.solution_md: β-1,4 from galactose to glucose — option (c).

questions.stem_md: Which of the following shows mutarotation when dissolved in water?

options.text_md: Trehalose, in which two glucose units are joined C1 to C1

questions.solution_md: Lactose keeps a free hemiacetal at C1 of its glucose unit; sucrose and trehalose use both anomeric carbons — option (a).

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** Lactose is a reducing sugar.

**Reason (R):** Lactose is made of galactose and glucose units.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: Both are true, but the reason for reducing power is the free hemiacetal at C1 of the glucose unit — option (b).

questions.stem_md: True or false? In sucrose, the glucose unit is present as a pyranose ring and the fructose unit as a furanose ring.
questions.solution_md: True.

questions.stem_md: The C–O–C link joining two monosaccharide units through an anomeric carbon, as in maltose, is called a ___ linkage.
questions.solution_md: **Glycosidic**.

questions.stem_md: Match each disaccharide with its glycosidic link.
questions.solution_md: Sucrose α1→β2; maltose α1→4; lactose β1→4 (galactose); cellobiose β1→4 (glucose).

questions.stem_md: Sucrose is hydrolysed completely to an equimolar mixture of D-glucose ($[\alpha]_D = +52.5^\circ$ at equilibrium) and D-fructose ($-92.4^\circ$). Taking the specific rotation of the mixture as the average of the two, calculate it.
questions.solution_md: $[\alpha]_D = \dfrac{52.5 - 92.4}{2} = -19.95^\circ$ (about $-20^\circ$): the sign has changed from $+$ to $-$, so the mixture is invert sugar.

questions.stem_md: Name the monosaccharide units and describe the glycosidic link in (a) maltose and (b) lactose. Are these sugars reducing?

answer.model_answer_md: (a) Maltose: two α-D-glucose units, C1 of one to C4 of the other (α-1,4). (b) Lactose: β-D-galactose and D-glucose, C1 of galactose to C4 of glucose (β-1,4). Both are reducing (free hemiacetal at C1 of the second unit).

questions.solution_md: Maltose α-1,4; lactose β-1,4; both reducing.

questions.stem_md: A solution of sucrose has a specific rotation of +66.5°. After warming with the enzyme invertase, the rotation is negative. Explain this change with an equation and name the product mixture.

answer.model_answer_md: $\ce{C12H22O11 + H2O ->[invertase] C6H12O6 + C6H12O6}$ (glucose + fructose). Glucose (+52.5°) is less dextrorotatory than fructose (−92.4°) is laevorotatory, so the equimolar mixture is laevorotatory (about −20°). The sign is inverted: invert sugar.

questions.solution_md: Hydrolysis; fructose dominates; invert sugar.

questions.stem_md: A disaccharide Z reduces Tollens’ reagent. The enzyme lactase hydrolyses it to D-galactose and D-glucose. (a) Identify Z. (b) Describe the glycosidic link in Z. (c) Explain why Z is a reducing sugar whereas sucrose is not.

answer.model_answer_md: (a) Lactose. (b) β-1,4: C1 of β-D-galactose to C4 of D-glucose. (c) In lactose C1 of the glucose unit is a free hemiacetal that can open to –CHO; in sucrose both anomeric carbons (C1 of glucose, C2 of fructose) are used in the link, so no ring can open.

questions.solution_md: Lactose; β-1,4; free hemiacetal.

questions.stem_md:
(a) What is a glycosidic linkage? [1]

(b) Name the monosaccharide units and describe the glycosidic link in (i) sucrose, (ii) maltose and (iii) lactose. [3]

(c) Explain why maltose is a reducing sugar but sucrose is not. [1]

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) The C–O–C (ether) link formed between the anomeric –OH of one monosaccharide and an –OH of another, with loss of water.

(b) (i) Sucrose: α-D-glucopyranose and β-D-fructofuranose, C1 of glucose to C2 of fructose (α1→β2). (ii) Maltose: two α-D-glucose units, C1 to C4 (α-1,4). (iii) Lactose: β-D-galactose and D-glucose, C1 of galactose to C4 of glucose (β-1,4).

(c) Maltose has a free hemiacetal at C1 of its second glucose unit, which opens to –CHO; in sucrose both anomeric carbons are in the link.

questions.solution_md: Definition; three structures; free hemiacetal.

questions.stem_md: Amylopectin, the major component of potato starch, differs from amylose in that amylopectin:

options.text_md: gives a deep blue colour with iodine and dissolves readily in water
has branches formed by α-1,6 links

questions.solution_md: Both use α-1,4 chains; amylopectin is branched through C6 — option (d).

questions.stem_md: After a meal, excess glucose in the body is stored in the liver and muscles as:

options.text_md: glycogen, a highly branched α-glucose polymer

questions.solution_md: Glycogen is animal starch — option (d).

questions.stem_md: Cotton fibres, almost pure cellulose, are strong and do not dissolve in water even though each glucose unit has free –OH groups. The main reason is that:

options.text_md: cellulose chains are highly branched like glycogen
straight β-1,4 chains lie side by side, held together by many hydrogen bonds
the –OH groups of cellulose are all acetylated

questions.solution_md: Inter-chain hydrogen bonding in parallel linear chains — option (c).

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** Glycogen can be broken down to glucose more rapidly than amylose.

**Reason (R):** Glycogen is highly branched, so it has many chain ends at which enzymes can act at the same time.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: Both are true, and R explains A — option (a).

questions.stem_md: True or false? Partial hydrolysis of starch by the enzyme diastase gives maltose.
questions.solution_md: True: starch → dextrins → maltose.

questions.stem_md: $48.6\ \text{g}$ of pure starch is hydrolysed completely with dilute acid. What mass of glucose ($M = 180$) is formed? (One chain unit, $\ce{C6H10O5}$, has $M = 162$.)
questions.solution_md: Units $= 48.6 \div 162 = 0.300\ \text{mol}$; mass of glucose $= 0.300 \times 180 = 54.0\ \text{g}$.

questions.stem_md: Give two differences between amylose and amylopectin.

answer.model_answer_md: Amylose is unbranched (α-1,4 only) while amylopectin is branched (α-1,4 chains with α-1,6 branches); amylose is soluble in hot water and gives a deep blue colour with iodine, while amylopectin is insoluble and gives a red-violet colour. (Amylose is 15–20% of starch, amylopectin 80–85%.)

questions.solution_md: Branching; solubility/iodine colour.

marking_scheme.step: Solubility or iodine colour or proportion

questions.stem_md: Compare starch, cellulose and glycogen with respect to (a) the glucose anomer present, (b) the glycosidic links and branching and (c) their function in living things.

answer.model_answer_md: (a) Starch and glycogen: α-D-glucose; cellulose: β-D-glucose. (b) Starch: α-1,4 (amylose) plus α-1,6 branches (amylopectin); glycogen: α-1,4 with more frequent α-1,6 branches; cellulose: unbranched β-1,4. (c) Starch: energy store in plants; glycogen: energy store in animals (liver, muscle); cellulose: structural material of plant cell walls.

questions.solution_md: Anomer; links and branching; function.

questions.stem_md:
(a) Describe the structure of starch, naming its two components and their glycosidic links. [2]

(b) Describe the structure of cellulose and explain why humans cannot digest it. [2]

(c) How does glycogen differ from amylopectin, and where is it stored? [1]

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) Starch = amylose (15–20%; unbranched chains of α-D-glucose, α-1,4 links; soluble; blue with iodine) + amylopectin (80–85%; α-1,4 chains branched by α-1,6 links about every 20–25 units; insoluble).

(b) Cellulose: unbranched chains of β-D-glucose with β-1,4 links; chains lie parallel and are hydrogen bonded into fibres. Human digestive enzymes hydrolyse only α-glycosidic links, so β-links are not broken.

(c) Glycogen is more highly branched (α-1,6 branches about every 8–12 units); it is stored in the liver and muscles of animals.

questions.solution_md: Amylose + amylopectin; β-1,4 cellulose; glycogen more branched.
